title: The Hubble Tension: Cosmology's Stubborn Crisis
hook: Two trustworthy ways of measuring how fast the universe expands keep disagreeing — and a decade of cross-checks has only hardened the gap into a genuine crisis.
key_points: The Hubble constant (H₀) measures how fast the universe is expanding today.
Early-universe data — the cosmic microwave background — give a lower H₀ than nearby measurements do.
Local measurements step outward with a 'distance ladder' of stars and Type Ia supernovae.
The gap exceeds known errors and has persisted for a decade across independent methods.
A local 'void' was ruled out; leading fixes alter the early universe or invoke new dark-energy physics.
content_html: How fast is the universe expanding right now? Two trustworthy ways of measuring that rate — the Hubble constant — keep giving different answers, and the gap is too big to blame on measurement error. After a decade of scrutiny, this "Hubble tension" has hardened from a curiosity into one of cosmology's deepest problems.
extra_html: One method reads the expansion rate off the early universe: the cosmic microwave background — the afterglow of the Big Bang — predicts a value once you assume the standard ΛCDM model. The other works outward from nearby space using a "distance ladder" of stars and exploding stars (Type Ia supernovae). The early-universe value comes out lower than the local one. In their decade review, Rong-Gen Cai and Shao-Jiang Wang note the disagreement survives whether or not the early measurement relies on Planck data, and whether or not the local one uses the distance ladder, and that a local "bubble" or void has been ruled out as the cause. That leaves uncomfortable options: shrink the early universe's "sound horizon," rethink how bright supernovae really are, or — the focus of their review — invoke new, possibly evolving dark-energy physics. See the full review for the competing fixes.

related.title: Is Dark Energy Changing Over Time?
related.hook: For decades dark energy looked like a constant. New galaxy-survey data hints it may evolve — and that would shift even our measured value of the cosmic expansion rate.

related.title: The Expanding Universe
related.hook: Distant galaxies are rushing away from us, and the farther one is, the faster it flees — not because they're moving through space, but because space itself is stretching.

related.title: Dark Energy Survives a Major Challenge
related.hook: A bold claim said the universe's accelerating expansion was an illusion. Astronomers checked the math, found the mistakes — and cosmic acceleration came out as strong as ever.

related.title: Dark Matter & Dark Energy
related.hook: Everything we can see — stars, planets, people — is only about 5% of the universe. The other 95% is two mysteries we've never directly detected.

flashcards.prompt: What does the 'Hubble tension' refer to?

choices.text: Early-universe and nearby measurements of the cosmic expansion rate disagree
Galaxies are receding faster than the speed of light
Telescopes can't agree on a single galaxy's exact distance

flashcards.explanation_html: The two well-established ways of measuring H₀ — from the early universe's afterglow and from the nearby distance ladder — give values that disagree by more than their error bars.

flashcards.prompt: Why is the Hubble tension treated as a real problem, not just noise?
flashcards.back_html: The disagreement is larger than the known measurement errors and persists across independent methods — whether or not the early estimate leans on Planck data, or the local one on the distance ladder.

flashcards.prompt: Which proposed explanation for the Hubble tension has been ruled out?

choices.text: That we sit in a local low-density 'bubble' or cosmic void
That the early universe's sound horizon was smaller than assumed
That dark energy might evolve over time

flashcards.explanation_html: A local Hubble bubble or void has long been excluded as a significant cause. Altering the early universe or invoking new dark-energy physics remain live options.
